lesson_title: Inflation and the CPI: The Trolley Behind the Number
hook_text: Your rent, your data, your bond and your bread all answer to one number. Here's the trolley it's built from.
clip_script: Picture one trolley packed to stand for every household in the country. What goes in? Whatever South Africans genuinely spend on: maize meal and cooking oil, a taxi-fare allowance, prepaid electricity, a data bundle, rent, school uniforms, a burial-society premium. Statistics South Africa did not guess this list — it asked thousands of households, and the answers decided the space each item occupies. Housing claims the biggest section. Every month, collectors price that exact same trolley again. In the starting year it cost R5 000 — stamp that 100. Three years later the identical trolley rings up R5 400. Divide, times 100: the stamp reads 108. That stamp is the CPI. Now the news number: last year the stamp said 108, today it says 114,5. It moved 6,5 points, and against the 108 where the year began, that is a 6 percent journey. That is the inflation rate. Not felt. Not voted on. One trolley, priced twice, compared. And when your family swears prices rose faster — both can be true. The official number is an average, and no real family is average.
visual_style: A lone trolley wheeling through twelve calendar pages, items sized by their basket weights; a till slip flipping from R5 000 to R5 400; a stamp thudding 100, then 108, then 114,5, before a bold 6,0% prints across the screen.
pacing: Calm build through the packing of the trolley, a snap on the divide-and-stamp move, warm landing on the average-versus-your-family twist.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read the next inflation headline like an economist — trolley, fire, hose and all.
